nodes.name: Update locking problem
nodes.statement: A commonly cited inefficiency of neural network training by back-propagation is the \textit{update locking} problem: each layer must wait for the signal to propagate through the full network before updating.
nodes.genus: inefficiency of neural network training by back-propagation
differentia: each layer must wait for the signal to propagate through the full network before updating

nodes.name: Backward unlocking
nodes.statement: Backward \textit{\textbf{un}locking} would permit updates of all modules once forward signals have propagated to all subsequent modules
nodes.genus: property of a training procedure permitting module updates
differentia: would permit updates of all modules once forward signals have propagated to all subsequent modules

nodes.name: Update unlocking
nodes.statement: update \textit{\textbf{un}locking} would permit updates of a module \textit{before} a signal has reached all subsequent modules
nodes.genus: property of a training procedure permitting module updates
differentia: would permit updates of a module \textit{before} a signal has reached all subsequent modules

nodes.name: Forward unlocking
nodes.statement: forward \textit{\textbf{un}locking} would permit a module to operate asynchronously from its predecessor and dependent modules.
nodes.genus: property of a training procedure permitting module updates

nodes.name: Decoupled Neural Interfaces (DNI)
nodes.statement: There, each network module has an associated \textit{auxiliary net} which, given the output activation of the module, predicts the gradient signal from subsequent modules: the module can thus perform an update while modules above are still forward processing.
nodes.statement_short: DNI: a per-module auxiliary net predicts the gradient coming from later modules, so the module can update immediately.
nodes.genus: network module associated to each network module
differentia: given the output activation of the module, predicts the gradient signal from subsequent modules

nodes.name: Per-module objective function $\hat{\mathcal{L}}$
nodes.statement: Let $\bm{X}_0$ and $Y$ be the data and labels, $\bm{X_j}$ be the output representation for module $j$. We will denote the per-module objective function $\hat{\mathcal{L}}(\bm{X}_{j}, Y;\theta_{j},\gamma_{j})$, where the parameters $\theta_j$ correspond to the module parameter (i.e. $\bm{X}_{j+1} =f_{\theta_{j}}(\bm{X}_{j})$). Here $\gamma_j$ represents parameters of a auxiliary networks used to predict the final target and compute the local objective. $\hat{\mathcal{L}}$ in our case will be the empirical risk with a cross-entropy loss.
nodes.statement_short: Notation for the local loss of module $j$ over module parameters $\theta_j$ and auxiliary parameters $\gamma_j$.
nodes.genus: empirical risk with a cross-entropy loss
differentia: the parameters $\theta_j$ correspond to the module parameter (i.e. $\bm{X}_{j+1} =f_{\theta_{j}}(\bm{X}_{j})$)
$\gamma_j$ represents parameters of a auxiliary networks used to predict the final target and compute the local objective

nodes.name: Stream of samples $\mathcal{S}$
nodes.statement: We mainly consider the online setting and assume a stream of samples or mini-batches denoted $\mathcal{S}\triangleq\{(x_0^t,y^t)\}_{t\leq T}$, run during $T$ iterations.
nodes.definiendum: stream of samples or mini-batches denoted $\mathcal{S}\triangleq\{(x_0^t,y^t)\}_{t\leq T}$

nodes.name: Replay buffer $B_j$ and its read/write protocol
nodes.statement: Each worker $j$ has a buffer that it writes to and that worker $j+1$ can read from. The buffer uses a simple read/write protocol. A buffer $B_j$ lets layer $j$ write new samples. When it reaches capacity it overwrites the oldest sample. Layer $j+1$ requests samples from the buffer $B_j$. They are selected by a last-in-first-out (LIFO) rule, with precedence for the least reused samples.
nodes.statement_short: Each worker owns a capacity-$M$ buffer; writes overwrite the oldest sample and reads are LIFO with preference for least-reused samples.
differentia: lets layer $j$ write new samples
When it reaches capacity it overwrites the oldest sample
They are selected by a last-in-first-out (LIFO) rule, with precedence for the least reused samples

nodes.name: Delay probability mass function $p(j)$
nodes.statement: Alg. \ref{algo:buffer_sym} simulates potential delays in such a setup by the use of a probability mass function (pmf) $p(j)$ over workers, analogous to typical asynchronous settings such as \citep{leblond2017asaga}. At each iteration, a layer is chosen at random according to $p(j)$ to perform a computation.
nodes.statement_short: Delays are simulated by drawing which worker computes at each iteration from a pmf $p(j)$ over workers.
differentia: over workers
At each iteration, a layer is chosen at random according to $p(j)$ to perform a computation

nodes.name: CNN-aux
nodes.section: 4.1 Other Approaches and Auxiliary Network Designs
nodes.origin_citation: Belilovsky et al. (shallow); Jaderberg et al. 2016
nodes.statement: The baseline auxiliary strategy based on \citep{shallow} and \citep{jaderberg2016decoupled} applies 2 CNN layers followed by a $2\times 2$ averaging and projection, denoted as \textit{CNN-aux}.
differentia: applies 2 CNN layers followed by a $2\times 2$ averaging and projection

nodes.name: MLP-aux
nodes.section: 4.1 Other Approaches and Auxiliary Network Designs
nodes.statement: First, we explore a direct application of the spatial averaging to $2\times2$ output shape (regardless of the resolution) followed by a 3-layer MLP (of constant width). This is denoted \textit{MLP-aux} and drastically reduces the FLOP count with minimal accuracy loss compared to \textit{CNN-aux}.

nodes.statement: Finally, we study a staged spatial resolution, first reducing the spatial resolution by 4$\times$ (and total size 16$\times$), then applying 3 $1\times 1$ convolutions followed by a reduction to $2\times 2$ and a 3 layer MLP, that we denote as \textit{MLP-SR-aux}.

nodes.name: Primary CIFAR-10 CNN architecture
nodes.section: 4.1 Other Approaches and Auxiliary Network Designs
nodes.statement: The primary network architecture we use for this study is a simple CNN similar to VGG family models \citep{simonyan2014very} and those used in \citep{shallow}. It consists of 6 convolutions of size $3\times 3$, batchnorm and shape preserving padding, with $2\times2$ maxpooling at layers 1 and 3. The width of the first layer is 128 and is doubled at each downsampling operation. The final layer does not have an auxiliary model-- it is followed by a pooling and 2-hidden layer fully connected network, for all experiments.
nodes.statement_short: A 6-layer VGG-style CNN with two maxpoolings, width 128 doubling at each downsample, and no auxiliary net on the last layer.
nodes.genus: simple CNN similar to VGG family models

nodes.name: Distance $c^t_{j-1}$ to the converged input density
nodes.statement: Let us fix a depth $j$, such that $j>1$ and consider the converged density of the previous layer, $p^*_{j-1}(z)$. We define the following distance: $c^t_{j-1}\triangleq \int |p_{j-1}^t(z)-p_{j-1}^*(z)|\,dz$.

nodes.statement: The greedy training objective is thus given recursively by defining $P_j$: \begin{equation} \min_{\theta_j,\gamma_j}\hat{\mathcal{L}}(\bm{X}_{j}, Y;\theta_{j},\gamma_{j})\tag{$P_j$}, \end{equation} where $\bm{X}_{j} =f_{\theta_{j-1}^*}(\bm{X}_{j-1})$ and $\theta_{j-1}^*$ is the minimizer of Problem (\(P_{j-1}\)).

nodes.name: Update unlocking scales better than backward unlocking
nodes.statement: However, update locking is a more severe inefficiency. Consider the case where each layer's forward processing time is $T_F$ and is equal across a network of $L$ layers. Given that the backward pass is a constant multiple in time of the forward, in the most ideal case the backward unlocking will still only scale as $\mathcal{O}(LT_F)$ with $L$ parallel nodes, while update unlocking could scale as $\mathcal{O}(T_F)$.
nodes.statement_short: Backward unlocking can at best reach $\mathcal{O}(LT_F)$, whereas update unlocking can reach $\mathcal{O}(T_F)$.

nodes.name: DGL is by construction faster than feedback-based methods
nodes.section: Detailed Discussion of Relative Speed of Competing Methods
nodes.statement: We will argue that if we take the assumption that each approach runs for the same number of epochs or iterations and applies the same splits of the network then DGL is by construction faster than the other methods which rely on feedback.
nodes.statement_short: At equal epochs and equal network splits, DGL is faster than any method that needs feedback.
assumptions: if we take the assumption that each approach runs for the same number of epochs or iterations and applies the same splits of the network
conclusions: DGL is by construction faster than the other methods which rely on feedback

nodes.name: Wall clock speedup over DDG
nodes.section: 4.1 Other Approaches and Auxiliary Network Designs
nodes.statement: We compare to the parallel implementation of \citep{ddg} using the same communication protocols and run on the same hardware. We find for $K=2,4$ GPU gives a $~5\%, 18\%$ respectively speedup over DDG. With DDG $K=4$ giving approximately $2.3\times$ speedup over standard backprop on same hardware (close to results from \citep{ddg}).
nodes.statement_short: DGL gives about 5% and 18% wall-clock speedup over DDG at $K=2$ and $K=4$.
assumptions: We compare to the parallel implementation of \citep{ddg} using the same communication protocols and run on the same hardware
conclusions: We find for $K=2,4$ GPU gives a $~5\%, 18\%$ respectively speedup over DDG

nodes.name: DGL reduces single-worker memory consumption
nodes.statement: Although not our focus, the single worker version of DGL has favorable memory usage compared to standard backprop training. For example, the ResNet-152 DGL $K=2$ setting can fit $38\%$ more samples on a single 16GB GPU than the standard end-to-end training.
nodes.statement_short: Even on a single worker DGL saves memory, fitting 38% more ResNet-152 samples on one 16GB GPU.
assumptions: the single worker version of DGL
the ResNet-152 DGL $K=2$ setting
conclusions: can fit $38\%$ more samples on a single 16GB GPU than the standard end-to-end training

nodes.name: DGL catches up with sequential greedy training
nodes.section: 4.1 Other Approaches and Auxiliary Network Designs
nodes.statement: Fig.~\ref{fig:greedy_v_parallel} shows comparisons of the learning curves for sequential training and DGL at layer 4 (layer 1 is the same for both as the input representation is not varying over the training period). DGL quickly catches up with the sequential training scheme and appears to sometimes generalize better.
nodes.statement_short: Parallel DGL matches sequential greedy learning curves and sometimes generalizes better.
assumptions: comparisons of the learning curves for sequential training and DGL at layer 4
conclusions: DGL quickly catches up with the sequential training scheme and appears to sometimes generalize better

nodes.name: DGL outperforms DNI and cDNI
nodes.section: 4.1 Other Approaches and Auxiliary Network Designs
nodes.statement: The DGL method outperforms DNI and the cDNI by a substantial amount both in test accuracy and training loss. Also in this setting, DGL can generalize better than standard backprop and obtains a close final training loss.
nodes.statement_short: On the reproduced CIFAR-10 DNI benchmark DGL beats DNI/cDNI and even generalizes better than backprop.

nodes.name: DGL matches end-to-end training on ImageNet
nodes.statement: We see that for all the models DGL can perform as well and sometimes better than the end-to-end trained models, while permitting parallel training. In all these cases the auxiliary networks are neglibile (see Appendix Table ~\ref{tab:flop_im} for more details). For the VGG-13 architecture we also evaluate the case where the model is trained layer by layer ($K=10$). Although here performance is slightly degraded, we find it is suprisingly high given that no backward communication is performed.
nodes.statement_short: On ImageNet, DGL matches or beats end-to-end backprop, and even fully layer-wise ($K=10$) VGG-13 degrades only slightly.
assumptions: the shortened optimization schedule prescribed in \citep{Xiao2019}
For the VGG-13 architecture we also evaluate the case where the model is trained layer by layer ($K=10$)

nodes.name: Async DGL accuracy is robust to worker slowdown
nodes.statement: First, observe that the accuracy of the synchronous algorithm is maintained in the setting where $S=1.0$ and the pmf is uniform. Note that even this is a non-trivial case, as it will mean that layers inherently have random delays (as compared to Alg. ~\ref{algo:basic}). Secondly, observe that accuracy is maintained until approximately $1.2\times$ and accuracy losses after that the difference remains small.
nodes.statement_short: Async DGL keeps synchronous accuracy up to a $1.2\times$ slowdown and degrades only mildly beyond it.
assumptions: the setting where $S=1.0$ and the pmf is uniform
conclusions: the accuracy of the synchronous algorithm is maintained
accuracy is maintained until approximately $1.2\times$ and accuracy losses after that the difference remains small

nodes.statement: We now consider the performance with respect to the buffer size. Results are shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:buffer2}. For this experiment we set $S=1.2\times$. Observe that even a tiny buffer size can yield only a slight loss in performance accuracy.
nodes.statement_short: Accuracy degrades only slightly even for very small replay buffers.
assumptions: For this experiment we set $S=1.2\times$
conclusions: even a tiny buffer size can yield only a slight loss in performance accuracy

nodes.name: Improved auxiliary models may further improve DGL
nodes.statement: We conjecture that improved auxiliary models and combinations with methods such as \citep{Huo2018} to allow feedback on top of the local model, may further improve performance.
assumptions: improved auxiliary models and combinations with methods such as \citep{Huo2018} to allow feedback on top of the local model

nodes.name: Combining async DGL with distributed synchronous SGD
nodes.statement: Combining asynchronous DGL with distributed synchronous SGD for sub-problem optimization is a promising direction. For example it can alleviate a common issue of the popular distributed synchronous SGD in deep CNNs, which is the often limiting maximum batch size \citep{im1hr}.
nodes.statement_short: Whether async DGL plus distributed synchronous SGD can lift the maximum-batch-size limit is left open.

nodes.name: Improving Async DGL with replay
nodes.statement: Building on this demonstration there are multiple directions to improve Async DGL with replay. For example improving the efficiency of the buffer~\cite{oyallon2018compressing}, by including data augmentation in feature space \citep{verma2018manifold}, mixing samples in batches, or improved batch sampling, among others.
nodes.statement_short: How best to make the replay buffer more efficient (compression, feature-space augmentation, batch mixing) is open.

nodes.name: Improved auxiliary problem objectives and delayed feedback
nodes.statement: Future work can develop improved auxiliary problem objectives and combinations with delayed feedback.

nodes.name: Sync-DGL generalizes a biologically plausible method
nodes.statement: Sync-DGL can also be seen as a generalization of the biologically plausible learning method proposed in concurrent work \citep{nokland2019training}.

nodes.name: Any iterative solver applies to the sub-problems
nodes.statement: In this work we solve the sub-problems $P_j$ by backpropagation, but we note that any iterative solver available for $P_j$ will be applicable (e.g. \cite{choromanska2018beyond}).

nodes.name: Time-varying sub-problem input distribution is unstudied
nodes.statement: Finally we emphasize that unlike the sequential solvers of (e.g. \citet{bengio2007greedy,shallow}) the distribution of inputs to each sub-problem solver changes over time, resulting in a learning dynamic whose properties have never been studied nor contrasted with sequential solvers.
nodes.statement_short: Unlike sequential greedy solvers, DGL sub-problems see a drifting input distribution whose dynamics are unstudied.

nodes.name: DGL converges in the standard sense
nodes.statement: Thus the DGL scheme converges in the sense of \citep{bottou2018optimization,Huo2018}.

nodes.name: Parallel setting adds a drift-controlled delay
nodes.statement: Thus compared to the sequential case, the parallel setting adds a delay that is controlled by $\sqrt{c_{j-1}^t}$.

nodes.name: Assumptions 1-3 are standard
nodes.statement: The Assumptions 1, 2 and 3 are standard \citep{bottou2018optimization, Huo2018}, and we show in the following that our proof of convergence leads to similar rates, up to a multiplicative constant.

nodes.name: Four factors governing relative speed
nodes.section: Detailed Discussion of Relative Speed of Competing Methods
nodes.statement: The relative speeds of these methods are governed by the following: \begin{enumerate} \item Computation besides forward and backward passes on primary network modules (e.g. auxiliary networks forward and backward passes) \item Communication time of sending activations from one module to the next module \item Communication time of sending feedback to the previous module \item Waiting time for signal to reach final module \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Relative speed depends on auxiliary computation, forward activation communication, feedback communication, and waiting for the top module.

nodes.name: Async DGL needs no master node
nodes.statement: Unlike common data-parallel asynchronous algorithms \citep{elasticSGD}, the asynchronous DGL does not rely on a master node and requires only local communication similar to recent decentralized schemes \citep{lian2017asynchronous}. Contrary to decentralized SGD, DGL nodes only need to maintain and update the parameters of their local module, permitting much larger modules.
nodes.statement_short: Async DGL is master-free, needs only neighbour communication, and each node stores only its own module.

nodes.name: $S=2.0$ is a drastic slowdown
nodes.statement: Note that even case $S=2.0$ is somewhat drastic: for 50 epochs, the slowed-down layer is only on epoch 25 while those following it are at epoch 50.

nodes.name: Auxiliary networks restricted to 5% of the main network
nodes.statement: The primary consideration is the relative speed of the auxiliary network with respect to its associated main network module. We will use primarily FLOP count in our analysis and aim to restrict our auxiliary networks to be $5\%$ of the main network.
nodes.statement_short: Design constraint: the auxiliary net should cost at most 5% of the main module's FLOPs.

nodes.name: Auxiliary network sizes for ImageNet VGG-13
nodes.section: Auxiliary Network Sizes and FLOP comparisons on ImageNet
nodes.statement: Lets take as an example the ImageNet experiments for VGG-13. At the first layer the output is $224\times224\times64$. The MLP-aux here would be applied after averaging to $2\times2\times 64$, and would consists of 3 fully connected layers of size $256$ ($2*2*64$) followed by a projection to $1000$ image categories. The MLP-SR-aux network used would first reduce to $56\times56\times64$ and then apply 3 layers of $1\times1$ convolutions of width 64. This is followed by reduction to $2\times2$ and 3 FC layers as in the MLP-aux network.
nodes.statement_short: Concrete MLP-aux and MLP-SR-aux instantiations for the first VGG-13 layer on ImageNet.

nodes.name: Synchronous DGL (Sync-DGL)
nodes.statement: \caption{Synchronous DGL} \SetAlgoLined \DontPrintSemicolon \KwIn{Stream $\mathcal{S}\triangleq\{(x_0^t,y^t)\}_{t\leq T}$ of samples or mini-batches.} \textbf{Initialize} Parameters $\{\theta_j,\gamma_j\}_{j\leq J}$.\; \For { $(x_0^t,y^t) \in \mathcal{S}$ } { \For {$j \in 1,..., J$} {$x^t_j \leftarrow f_{\theta_{j-1}}(x^t_{j-1})$.\; Compute $\nabla_{(\gamma_j,\theta_j)}\hat{ \mathcal{L}}(y^t,x^t_j;\gamma_j,\theta_j)$.\; $(\theta_j,\gamma_j)\leftarrow$Update parameters $(\theta_j,\gamma_j)$. } }
nodes.statement_short: Every layer, in parallel, forwards its mini-batch to the next layer and immediately updates from its own local auxiliary loss.

nodes.name: Asynchronous DGL with Replay
nodes.statement: \SetAlgoLined \DontPrintSemicolon \KwIn{Stream $\mathcal{S}\triangleq\{(x_0^t,y^t)\}_{t\leq T}$; Distribution of the delay $p=\{p(j)\}_{j}$; Buffer size $M$.} \textbf{Initialize:} Buffers $\{B_j\}_{j}$; params $\{\theta_j,\gamma_j\}_{j}$.\\ \While{\normalfont{\textbf{ training}}}{Sample $j$ in $\{1,...,J\}$ following $p$.\\ \uIf{$j=1$}{ $ (x_{0},y)\gets \mathcal{S}$}\Else{ $(x_{j-1},y)\gets B_{j-1}$.} $x_j \leftarrow f_{\theta_{j-1}}(x_{j-1})$.\; Compute $\nabla_{(\gamma_j,\theta_j)}\hat{ \mathcal{L}}(y,x_j;\gamma_j,\theta_j)$.\; $(\theta_j,\gamma_j)\leftarrow$ Update parameters $(\theta_j,\gamma_j)$.\; \lIf{$j<J$}{ $B_{j} \gets (x^{j},y)$. }} \caption{Asynchronous DGL with Replay}
nodes.statement_short: At each iteration a randomly chosen worker reads from its predecessor's replay buffer, updates locally, and writes its output to its own buffer.

nodes.name: Sequential solution of the greedy objective
nodes.origin_citation: Bengio et al. 2007; Belilovsky et al. (shallow); Huang et al. 2017; Marquez et al.
nodes.statement: A natural way to solve the optimization problem for $J$ modules, $(P_J)$, is thus by sequentially solving the problems $\{P_{j}\}_{j\leq J}$ starting with $j=1$. This is the approach taken in e.g. \citet{Marquez,huang2017learning,bengio2007greedy,shallow}.
nodes.statement_short: Baseline: fully optimize each module's sub-problem in order, from the first layer upward.

nodes.name: DGL Parallel Implementation
nodes.statement: \caption{DGL Parallel Implementation} \SetAlgoLined \DontPrintSemicolon \KwIn{Stream $\mathcal{S}\triangleq\{(x_0^t,y^t)\}_{t\leq T}$ of samples or mini-batches;} \textbf{Initialize} Parameters $\{\theta_j,\gamma_j\}_{j\leq J}$\\ Worker 0:\; \For {$x_0^t \in \mathcal{S}$}{ $x^t_1 \leftarrow f_{\theta^t_{0}}(x^t_{0})$\\ Send $x_0^t$ to worker $1$\; Compute $\nabla_{(\gamma_1,\theta_1)}\hat{ \mathcal{L}}(y^t,x^t_0;\gamma^t_0,\theta^t_0)$\; $(\theta^{t+1}_0,\gamma^{t+1}_0)\leftarrow$ Step of parameters $(\theta^t_0,\gamma^t_0)$} Worker $j$:\; \For{$t \in 0 ... T$}{ Wait until $x^t_{j-1}$ is available\; $x^t_j \leftarrow f_{\theta^t_{j-1}}(x^t_{j-1})$ \\ Compute $\nabla_{(\gamma_j,\theta_j)}\hat{ \mathcal{L}}(y^t,x^t_j;\gamma^t_j,\theta^t_j)$\\ Send $x^t_{j}$ to worker $x^t_{j+1}$\\ $(\theta^{t+1}_j,\gamma^{t+1}_j)\leftarrow$ Step of parameters $(\theta^t_j,\gamma^t_j)$}

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.1
nodes.statement:
First of all, observe that under Assumption 4 and via Fubini's theorem:  egin{equation} \sum_t c_{j-1}^t = \sum_t \int |p_{j-1}^t(z)-p_{j-1}^*(z)|\,dz=\int\sum_t |p_{j-1}^t(z)-p_{j-1}^*(z)|\,dz <\infty \end{equation} thus, $\sum_t |p_j^t-p_j^*|$ is convergent a.s. and $|p_j^t-p_j^*|ightarrow 0$ a.s as well. From Fatou's lemma, one has:  egin{align} \int p^*_{j-1}(z)\Vert
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(z;\Theta_j)\Vert^2 \,dz&= \int \lim\inf_t p^t_{j-1}(z)\Vert
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(z;\Theta_j)\Vert^2 \,dz\ &\leq \lim\inf_t \int p^t_{j-1}(z)\Vert
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(z;\Theta_j)\Vert^2 \,dz\leq G \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Fubini gives summable total variation, hence $p^t_{j-1}\to p^*_{j-1}$ a.s.; then Fatou's lemma transfers the bound $G$ to the limit density.

nodes.name: Fubini's theorem gives summable total variation
nodes.statement: First of all, observe that under Assumption 4 and via Fubini's theorem: \begin{equation} \sum_t c_{j-1}^t = \sum_t \int |p_{j-1}^t(z)-p_{j-1}^*(z)|\,dz=\int\sum_t |p_{j-1}^t(z)-p_{j-1}^*(z)|\,dz <\infty \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Swap sum and integral by Fubini to get $\sum_t c_{j-1}^t<\infty$.

nodes.name: Almost sure convergence of the densities
nodes.statement: thus, $\sum_t |p_j^t-p_j^*|$ is convergent a.s. and $|p_j^t-p_j^*|\rightarrow 0$ a.s as well.

nodes.name: Fatou's lemma bounds the limiting second moment
nodes.statement:
From Fatou's lemma, one has:  egin{align} \int p^*_{j-1}(z)\Vert
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(z;\Theta_j)\Vert^2 \,dz&= \int \lim\inf_t p^t_{j-1}(z)\Vert
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(z;\Theta_j)\Vert^2 \,dz\ &\leq \lim\inf_t \int p^t_{j-1}(z)\Vert
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(z;\Theta_j)\Vert^2 \,dz\leq G \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Apply Fatou's lemma and Assumption 3 to conclude the bound $G$ under $p^*_{j-1}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.2
nodes.statement:
By $L$-smoothness:  egin{align} \mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^{t+1})\leq\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)&+
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)^{T}(\Theta^{t+1}_{j}-\Theta_{j}^t)+ rac{L}{2}\Vert\Theta_{j}^{t+1}-\Theta_{j}^t\Vert^{2} \end{align} Substituting $\Theta_{j}^{t+1}-\Theta_{j}^{t}$ on the right:  egin{align} \mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^{t+1})&\leq\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)-\eta_t
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)^{T} 
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z_{j-1}^t;\Theta_j^t)+ rac{L\eta_t^2}{2}\Vert
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z_{j-1}^t;\Theta_j^t)\Vert^{2} \end{align} Taking the expectation w.r.t. $Z_{j-1}^t$ which has a density $p_{j-1}^t$, we get:  egin{align*} \mathbb{E}_{p^t_{j-1}}[\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^{t+1})]&\leq\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)-\eta_t
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{j-1}^t}[
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z_{j-1}^t;\Theta_j^t)] + rac{L\eta_t^2}{2}\mathbb{E}_{p_{j-1}^t} ig[\Vert
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z_{j-1}^t;\Theta_j^t)\Vert^{2} ig] \end{align*} From Assumption 3, we obtain that:  egin{equation}  rac{L\eta_t^2}{2}\mathbb{E}_{p_{j-1}^t} ig[\Vert 
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z_{j-1}^t;\Theta_j^t)\Vert^{2} ig]\leq  rac{L\eta_t^2G}{2} \end{equation} Then, as a side computation, observe that:  egin{align} \Vert \mathbb{E}_{p_{j-1}^t} ig[
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z_{j-1}^t;\Theta_j^t) ig]-
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)\Vert&=\Vert \int 
abla \ell(z,\Theta_j^t)p^t_{j-1}(z)\,d z -\int 
abla \ell(z,\Theta_j^t)p^*_{j-1}(z)\,d z\Vert\ &\leq \int \Vert
abla \ell(z,\Theta_j^t)\Vert ~ |p^t_{j-1}(z)-p^*_{j-1}(z)|\,d z\ &= \int  ig(\Vert
abla \ell(z,\Theta_j^t)\Vert\sqrt{|p^t_{j-1}(z)-p^*_{j-1}(z)|} ig) ~ \sqrt{|p^t_{j-1}(z)-p^*_{j-1}(z)|}\,d z\ \end{align} Let us apply the Cauchy-Swchartz inequality, we obtain:  egin{align} \Vert \mathbb{E}_{p_{j-1}^t} ig[
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z_{j-1}^t;\Theta_j^t) ig]-
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)\Vert&\leq \sqrt{\int \Vert
abla \ell(z,\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2 |p^t_{j-1}(z)-p^*_{j-1}(z)|\,d z} \sqrt{\int |p^t_{j-1}(z)-p^*_{j-1}(z)|\,d z }\ &= \sqrt{\int \Vert
abla \ell(z,\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2 |p^t_{j-1}(z)-p^*_{j-1}(z)|\,d z} \sqrt{c_{j-1}^t} \end{align} Then, observe that:  egin{align} \int \Vert
abla \ell(z,\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2 |p^t_{j-1}(z)-p^*_{j-1}(z)|\,d z &\leq \int \Vert
abla \ell(z,\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2  ig(p^t_{j-1}(z)+p^*_{j-1}(z) ig)\,d z\ &=\mathbb{E}_{p^t_{j-1}}[ \Vert
abla \ell(Z_{j-1},\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2 ]+\mathbb{E}_{p^*_{j-1}}[ \Vert
abla \ell(Z_{j-1},\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2 ]\ &\leq 2G \end{align} The last inequality follows from Lemma 4.1 and Assumption 3. Then, using again Cauchy-Schwartz inequality:  egin{align}  igg|\Vert
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2- 
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{j-1}^t}[
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z_{j-1}^t;\Theta_j^t)] igg| &= igg|
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)^T ig(
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)-\mathbb{E}_{p_{j-1}^t}[
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z_{j-1}^t;\Theta_j^t)] ig) igg|\ &\leq \Vert 
abla \mathcal{L}(\Theta^t_j)\Vert~\Vert \mathbb{E}_{p_{j-1}^t} ig[
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z_{j-1}^t;\Theta_j^t) ig]-
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)\Vert \ &\leq \Vert 
abla \mathcal{L}(\Theta^t_j)\Vert \sqrt{2Gc^t_{j-1}} \end{align} Then, taking the expectation leads to  egin{align}  ig|\mathbb{E} igg[\Vert
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2- 
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{j-1}^t}[
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z_{j-1}^t;\Theta_j^t)] igg] ig|&\leq \mathbb{E}[ igg|\Vert
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2- 
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{j-1}^t}[
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z_{j-1}^t;\Theta_j^t)] igg|]\ &\leq \mathbb{E}[\Vert
abla \mathcal{L}(\Theta^t_j)\Vert] \sqrt{2Gc^t_{j-1}}\ &\leq \sqrt{ \mathbb{E}[\Vert
abla \mathcal{L}(\Theta^t_j)\Vert^2] }\sqrt{2Gc^t_{j-1}}\ \end{align} However, observe that by Lemma 4.1 and Jensen inequality:  egin{align} \Vert 
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2 =\Vert \mathbb{E}_{p^*_j}[
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z,\Theta_j^t)]\Vert^2\leq \mathbb{E}_{p^*_j}[ \Vert 
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z,\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2]\leq G \end{align} Combining this inequality and Assumption 3, we get:  egin{align*} \mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^{t+1})]\leq\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^{t})]-\eta_t ig(\mathbb{E}[\Vert
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2]-\sqrt{2}Gc^t_{j-1} ig)+ rac{LG}{2}\eta_t^2\,, \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Descent lemma from $L$-smoothness, then two Cauchy-Schwarz bounds on the gradient bias induced by the input-density mismatch $c^t_{j-1}$.

nodes.name: Expand by $L$-smoothness
nodes.statement: By $L$-smoothness: \begin{align} \mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^{t+1})\leq\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)&+\nabla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)^{T}(\Theta^{t+1}_{j}-\Theta_{j}^t)+\frac{L}{2}\Vert\Theta_{j}^{t+1}-\Theta_{j}^t\Vert^{2} \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Start from the descent lemma implied by $L$-smoothness of $\mathcal{L}$.

nodes.name: Substitute the SGD increment
nodes.statement_short: Replace the parameter increment by the SGD update $-\eta_t\nabla_{\Theta_j}\ell$.

nodes.name: Take expectation under the current density
nodes.statement:
Taking the expectation w.r.t. $Z_{j-1}^t$ which has a density $p_{j-1}^t$, we get:  egin{align*} \mathbb{E}_{p^t_{j-1}}[\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^{t+1})]&\leq\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)-\eta_t
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{j-1}^t}[
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z_{j-1}^t;\Theta_j^t)] + rac{L\eta_t^2}{2}\mathbb{E}_{p_{j-1}^t} ig[\Vert
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z_{j-1}^t;\Theta_j^t)\Vert^{2} ig] \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Average over the time-$t$ input density $p^t_{j-1}$.

nodes.name: Bound the second-order term by Assumption 3
nodes.statement: From Assumption 3, we obtain that: \begin{equation} \frac{L\eta_t^2}{2}\mathbb{E}_{p_{j-1}^t}\big[\Vert \nabla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z_{j-1}^t;\Theta_j^t)\Vert^{2}\big]\leq \frac{L\eta_t^2G}{2} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Use the finite-variance assumption to bound the quadratic term by $L\eta_t^2G/2$.

nodes.name: Side computation: gradient bias from the density mismatch
nodes.statement:
Then, as a side computation, observe that:  egin{align} \Vert \mathbb{E}_{p_{j-1}^t} ig[
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z_{j-1}^t;\Theta_j^t) ig]-
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)\Vert&=\Vert \int 
abla \ell(z,\Theta_j^t)p^t_{j-1}(z)\,d z -\int 
abla \ell(z,\Theta_j^t)p^*_{j-1}(z)\,d z\Vert\ &\leq \int \Vert
abla \ell(z,\Theta_j^t)\Vert ~ |p^t_{j-1}(z)-p^*_{j-1}(z)|\,d z\ &= \int  ig(\Vert
abla \ell(z,\Theta_j^t)\Vert\sqrt{|p^t_{j-1}(z)-p^*_{j-1}(z)|} ig) ~ \sqrt{|p^t_{j-1}(z)-p^*_{j-1}(z)|}\,d z\ \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Write the gradient bias as an integral against $|p^t_{j-1}-p^*_{j-1}|$ split into two square-root factors.

nodes.name: Apply Cauchy-Schwarz to the bias integral
nodes.statement:
Let us apply the Cauchy-Swchartz inequality, we obtain:  egin{align} \Vert \mathbb{E}_{p_{j-1}^t} ig[
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z_{j-1}^t;\Theta_j^t) ig]-
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)\Vert&\leq \sqrt{\int \Vert
abla \ell(z,\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2 |p^t_{j-1}(z)-p^*_{j-1}(z)|\,d z} \sqrt{\int |p^t_{j-1}(z)-p^*_{j-1}(z)|\,d z }\ &= \sqrt{\int \Vert
abla \ell(z,\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2 |p^t_{j-1}(z)-p^*_{j-1}(z)|\,d z} \sqrt{c_{j-1}^t} \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy-Schwarz factors out $\sqrt{c_{j-1}^t}$.

nodes.name: Bound the remaining integral by $2G$
nodes.statement:
Then, observe that:  egin{align} \int \Vert
abla \ell(z,\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2 |p^t_{j-1}(z)-p^*_{j-1}(z)|\,d z &\leq \int \Vert
abla \ell(z,\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2  ig(p^t_{j-1}(z)+p^*_{j-1}(z) ig)\,d z\ &=\mathbb{E}_{p^t_{j-1}}[ \Vert
abla \ell(Z_{j-1},\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2 ]+\mathbb{E}_{p^*_{j-1}}[ \Vert
abla \ell(Z_{j-1},\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2 ]\ &\leq 2G \end{align} The last inequality follows from Lemma 4.1 and Assumption 3.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the mismatch integral by the sum of the two second moments, i.e. $2G$, via Lemma 4.1 and Assumption 3.

nodes.name: Second Cauchy-Schwarz on the inner product
nodes.statement:
Then, using again Cauchy-Schwartz inequality:  egin{align}  igg|\Vert
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2- 
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{j-1}^t}[
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z_{j-1}^t;\Theta_j^t)] igg| &= igg|
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)^T ig(
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)-\mathbb{E}_{p_{j-1}^t}[
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z_{j-1}^t;\Theta_j^t)] ig) igg|\ &\leq \Vert 
abla \mathcal{L}(\Theta^t_j)\Vert~\Vert \mathbb{E}_{p_{j-1}^t} ig[
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z_{j-1}^t;\Theta_j^t) ig]-
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)\Vert \ &\leq \Vert 
abla \mathcal{L}(\Theta^t_j)\Vert \sqrt{2Gc^t_{j-1}} \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Control the difference between the true and sampled inner products by $\Vert\nabla\mathcal{L}\Vert\sqrt{2Gc^t_{j-1}}$.

nodes.name: Take expectation and use Jensen
nodes.statement:
Then, taking the expectation leads to  egin{align}  ig|\mathbb{E} igg[\Vert
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2- 
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{j-1}^t}[
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z_{j-1}^t;\Theta_j^t)] igg] ig|&\leq \mathbb{E}[ igg|\Vert
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2- 
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{j-1}^t}[
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z_{j-1}^t;\Theta_j^t)] igg|]\ &\leq \mathbb{E}[\Vert
abla \mathcal{L}(\Theta^t_j)\Vert] \sqrt{2Gc^t_{j-1}}\ &\leq \sqrt{ \mathbb{E}[\Vert
abla \mathcal{L}(\Theta^t_j)\Vert^2] }\sqrt{2Gc^t_{j-1}}\ \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Move to expectations and apply Jensen to replace $\mathbb{E}\Vert\nabla\mathcal{L}\Vert$ by its root second moment.

nodes.name: Bound the expected gradient norm by $G$
nodes.statement:
However, observe that by Lemma 4.1 and Jensen inequality:  egin{align} \Vert 
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2 =\Vert \mathbb{E}_{p^*_j}[
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z,\Theta_j^t)]\Vert^2\leq \mathbb{E}_{p^*_j}[ \Vert 
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z,\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2]\leq G \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Jensen plus Lemma 4.1 give $\Vert\nabla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2\leq G$.

nodes.name: Combine into the descent inequality
nodes.statement: Combining this inequality and Assumption 3, we get: \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^{t+1})]\leq\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^{t})]-\eta_t\big(\mathbb{E}[\Vert\nabla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2]-\sqrt{2}Gc^t_{j-1}\big)+\frac{LG}{2}\eta_t^2\,, \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Assemble all bounds into the claimed one-step descent inequality.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.2
nodes.statement: Applying Lemma \ref{lemma:main} for $t=0,...,T-1$, we obtain (observe the telescoping sum), for our non-negative loss: \begin{align}\sum_{t=0}^T \eta_t \mathbb{E}[\Vert\nabla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2]& \leq \mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}(\Theta^0_j)]-\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}(\Theta^{T+1}_j)] +\sqrt 2G\sum_{t=0}^T\sqrt{c_j^t}\eta_t +\frac{LG}{2}\sum_{t=0}^T \eta_t^2\\ &\leq \mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}(\Theta^0_j)] +\sqrt 2G\sum_{t=0}^T\sqrt{c_j^t}\eta_t +\frac{LG}{2}\sum_{t=0}^T \eta_t^2\\ \end{align} Yet, $\sum \sqrt{c_j^t}\eta_t$ is convergent, as $\sum c_j^t$ and $\sum_t \eta_t^2$ are convergent, thus the right term is bounded.
nodes.statement_short: Telescoping sum of Lemma 4.2 over $t$, then boundedness of $\sum\sqrt{c_j^t}\eta_t$ and $\sum\eta_t^2$.

nodes.name: Telescope the per-step descent inequality
nodes.statement: Applying Lemma \ref{lemma:main} for $t=0,...,T-1$, we obtain (observe the telescoping sum), for our non-negative loss: \begin{align}\sum_{t=0}^T \eta_t \mathbb{E}[\Vert\nabla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2]& \leq \mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}(\Theta^0_j)]-\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}(\Theta^{T+1}_j)] +\sqrt 2G\sum_{t=0}^T\sqrt{c_j^t}\eta_t +\frac{LG}{2}\sum_{t=0}^T \eta_t^2\\ &\leq \mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}(\Theta^0_j)] +\sqrt 2G\sum_{t=0}^T\sqrt{c_j^t}\eta_t +\frac{LG}{2}\sum_{t=0}^T \eta_t^2\\ \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Sum Lemma 4.2 over $t$ and drop the non-negative final loss term.

nodes.name: Conclude boundedness of the right-hand side
nodes.statement: Yet, $\sum \sqrt{c_j^t}\eta_t$ is convergent, as $\sum c_j^t$ and $\sum_t \eta_t^2$ are convergent, thus the right term is bounded.
nodes.statement_short: Robbins-Monro and Assumption 4 make the right-hand side finite.

nodes.name: Argument that DGL is faster by construction
nodes.section: Detailed Discussion of Relative Speed of Competing Methods
nodes.statement: As discussed in the text our auxiliary modules which govern (1) for DGL are negligible thus the overhead of (1) is negligible. DNI will inherently have large auxiliary models as it must predict gradients, thus (1) will be much greater than in DGL. (2) should be of equal speed across all methods given the same implementation and hardware. (3) does not exist for the case of DGL but exists for all other cases. (4) applies only in the case of backward unlocking methods (DDG/FA) and does not exist for DNI or DGL as they are update unlocked. Thus we observe that DGL by construction is faster than the other methods.
